(1) there are differences among ND vaccine isolates in their ability to stimulate HI and VN titers in chickens; and (2) the differences in HI and VN titres are due to differences in the hemagglutinin and neuraminidase genes.

the immunological differences among these NDV strains were not great enough to warrant a significant change in the current vaccine recommendations.

A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

, in general, all the vaccine strains were of equal immunogenic potential and that, in the absence of a standardization program, the selection of vaccine strains for use in the field should be made on the basis of cost, availability, and the experience of the producer with a particular strain.

the majority of the vaccine strains studied proved to be of similar immunogenicity and that, in the majority of instances, commercial vaccines were of comparable potency to those strains not used commercially.
there is a great variation of immunogenic potential among the strains of NDV evaluated in this study.
The main takeaway from our work is that

the immunogenicity of a particular vaccine isolate may be different from the immunogenicity expected from a particular vaccine designation, and the immunogenicity should be evaluated before use in the field.

the immunogenic potential of a given NDV vaccine strain may vary from that of other isolates of the same strain designation, and the immunological response may vary from that anticipated from the use of a given vaccine strain.
the immunogenicity of ND vaccine viruses can vary considerably and that this variation can have important ramifications for vaccine selection.
